WARNING

The court hearing this matter directs that the
following notice should be attached to the file:

This is a case under
Part V of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
, (being Schedule
1 to the
Supporting Children, Youth and Families Act, 2017
, S.O. 2017,
c. 14), and is subject to subsections 87(7), 87(8) and 87(9) of the Act.
These subsections and subsection 142(3)
of
the Act, which
deals
with the consequences of failure to comply, read as follows:

87.—
(7)
Order
excluding media representatives or prohibiting publication.
—   Where
the court is of the opinion that the presence of the media representative or
representatives or the publication of the report, as the case may be, would
cause emotional harm to a child who is a witness at or a participant in the
hearing or is the subject of the proceeding, the court may make an order,

.  .  .

(
c
)    prohibiting
the publication of a report of the hearing or a specified part of the hearing.

(8)
Prohibition
re identifying child.
—   No person shall publish or make
public information that has the effect of identifying a child who is a witness
at or a participant in a hearing or the subject of a proceeding, or the child’s
parent or foster parent or a member of the child’s family.

(9)
Prohibition
re identifying person charged
.—   The court may make an
order prohibiting the publication of information that has the effect of
identifying a person charged with an offence under this Part.

.  .  .

142.—
(3)
Offences
re publication.
—   A person who contravenes subsection 87(8)
or 134(11) (publication of identifying information) or an order prohibiting
publication made under clause 87(7)(
c
) or subsection 87(9), and a
director, officer or employee of a corporation who authorizes, permits or
concurs in such a contravention by the corporation, is guilty of an offence and
on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment
for a term of not more than three years, or to both.

ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE

BONDY, J.:

REASONS

Introduction:

[
1
]

This is a Protection Application that was commenced January 25
th
,
2021.  The Applicant is the Windsor- Essex Children’s Aid Society (Hereinafter
the
“
Society
”).

The child who is the subject of these proceedings is A.D. who was born […],
2014.

[
2
]

His parents are J.S. (the “Mother”) and M.D. (the “Father”). The parties
to this Protection Application are the parents and the Walpole Island First
Nation as A.D. and the Mother are band members. The Office of the Children’s
Lawyer represented A.D. throughout these proceedings.

[
3
]

The Society seeks a finding of protection under s. 74 (2) (h) of the
CYFSA

which reads that a child is in need of protection when
“there is a risk that
the child(ren) is/are likely to suffer emotional harm, demonstrated by serious
anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive or aggressive behaviour, or
delayed development resulting from the actions, failure to act or pattern of
neglect on the part of the child(ren’s) parent or the person having charge of
the child(ren)”.

[
4
]

In the event of that finding, the Society by its Answer seeks an Order
having the child remain in the care of his Mother, subject to terms of
supervised access to the Father.

[
5
]

The Mother by her Answer concurs with this request.

[
6
]

The Office of the Children’s Lawyer concurs with that request.

[
7
]

The Walpole First Nation concurs also.

[
8
]

The Father by his Answer seeks a dismissal of the Protection Application
stating there is no basis to the finding of protection sought and seeks an Order
that A.D. remain with his Mother subject to supervision of the Society with
unsupervised access to the Father.

[
9
]

Given the complexity of the evidence, I conducted a bifurcated hearing
with the evidence relating to protection only being first heard.  This is my Ruling
and Reasons on that finding.

Background:

[
10
]

A.D.’s
parents were never married, they resided together for a period of time and
ultimately separated sometime around 2017.  They have been involved in
litigation ever since that separation relating to issues of custody and access
(now described as decision making and parenting time) of A.D.  An Application
under the
Children’s Law Reform Act
resulted in an Order of custody to
the Mother made by Tobin J. on May 18
th
, 2018.  I issued a consent Order
on June 18
th
, 2019, providing the Father with supervised access on
alternate Sundays. The parties had attended for mediation and resolved the
issue of the Father’s access even though a trial of the issue had been directed
by Tobin J.

[
11
]

By
2019, competing Motions to Change were initiated by the Mother and Father as
the party supervising A.D.’s access was no longer willing to do so. I gather
that the loss of this supervisor and the Father’s corresponding loss of access
time to A.D.  generated this new litigation.  By interim Order of December 16
th
,
2019, Vickerd J. varied my Order and allowed for two other persons to supervise
the Father’s visitation to A.D., namely, A.D.’s grandmother and uncle.

[
12
]

On
March 27
th
, 2020, Phillips J. made a further Order varying the
interim Order of Vickerd J. in the face of cross motions and competing
conflictual Affidavits by the Mother and Father.  Justice Phillips’ Reasons are
detailed and instructive.  He noted that Tobin J. had stated that “
The
Father fairly and candidly stated that he is not opposed to Ms. S. having
custody of the child. What he wants is an opportunity to play a significant
role in the life of his child.
” He noted that my final Order of June 18
th
,
2019, was on consent.  He noted that on both occasions, the Father chose to
concur in a Consent and did not engage in litigation.

[
13
]

He
also noted that Vickerd J. had previously made an Order for the appointment of
the Children’s Lawyer which resulted in an investigation being pursued. She
dismissed the Father’s interim claim for custody before her.   A CAS
investigation at that time was noted as identifying post separation conflict as
being “verified” but
“A.D. [does] not appear to be overly affected at this
point.
”  He also noted the dismissal of criminal proceedings against the
Father in which the Mother was the Complainant. He noted that some of those
charges were dismissed, one was withdrawn and there was a Crown request to
dismiss the remaining counts.  He considered that direction by the Crown as
“remarkable” and “exceptional”, but his reasons do not elaborate what evidence
was before him to draw that conclusion.  He noted specifically that the
Father’s Form 35.1 Affidavit before him revealed no criminal record or pending
criminal charges.  In the face of the pandemic and the unworkable arrangements
related to exercising access at a community-based access centre and the
evidence that A.D. was enjoying time with his Father, he allowed for both
compensatory and unsupervised access by the Father to A.D. I note with emphasis
“
provided that his Father does not expose his son to the ugliness of the
custody and access litigation”.

[
14
]

He
also said this:
“If this child is at risk, it is in consequence of being at
the center of a litigation war between his parents.  A.D. must not be caught in
the crossfire. Both the adults are culpable in this respect”.

[
15
]

A
trial of the issues addressed in the competing Motions to Change was heard by
Ross J. on October 19
th
, 20
th
and 21
st
of
2020.   Justice Ross’ Reasons of June 2
nd
, 2020, reflect that she
faced a confusing quagmire of proceedings, evidence and positions advanced by
the Mother and Father.  Nonetheless, her Reasons are detailed and instructive.

[
16
]

Her
findings note that there was general disagreement between the Mother and Father
about the periods of time they lived together, how well or how poorly A.D. was
taken care of, why they separated and who was the primary parent during the
time they lived together.  By the time of the hearing, the Mother was proposing
unsupervised access to the Father, however her trial testimony and her original
Motion to Change sought supervision over the Father’s access as the Mother
claimed she was fearful of the Father and her son. Justice Ross noted that at
the same time the Mother did not give any evidence or call any evidence from a
third party as to why, after several months of unsupervised access, she was now
seeking supervised access.  These were deficiencies noted by Justice Ross.

[
17
]

In
commenting on the Father, Justice Ross opined that
“ [the Father] simply
could not turn his attention to the issues at hand. I formed the distinct
impression that [the Father’s] anger and loathing for the [Mother] overshadowed
his ability to consider the decision the court was being asked to make
.”
She also found, and I emphasize that “[
the Father’s] obsession with what he
perceived as wrongdoing against him by [the Mother] completely prevented him
from putting his best foot forward as a parent”.
Justice Ross was
referring to the criminal charges that the Father had faced where the Mother
was the Complainant and his ongoing concern how that would impact his claims.
She also found that the Father could or would not make a connection between how
his request for every Saturday access may be interfering with his son’s
connection to Walpole Island and his First Nation community there. During the
trial, the Judge noted that as it related to this request (that A.D. spend time
at Walpole Island and the activities there) the Father became visibly and
verbally upset, shouting out that “he was tired of the racism”.

[
18
]

Justice
Ross also found that there was commonality between the parties and their
witnesses that there were often (perhaps always) some kind of verbal dispute
during the access exchanges, with reports of police being called and the Father
shouting at third parties present.  She found that
“the takeaway from all of
this evidence about these loud shouting matches is that [A.D.] was present for
all of them. It is hard to imagine how this little boy was feeling about
watching his parents and the other adults shout and threaten one another every
time he went for access with his dad and when he came back.”
Most
importantly, she found that “
Neither parent was able to explain the problem
to me. Sadly, neither parent seemed to have any insight as to how their
behaviour was impacting their son”.

[
19
]

In
conclusion, Ross J. kept A.D.’s custody/decision making with his Mother with
unsupervised access to the Father. She provided that he could decide what “one”
extracurricular activity A.D. could engage in. She expressed that she found it
was important for A.D. to have weekend time with his Mother, which weekend time
would include the Walpole Island activities.  Her Order provided for a detailed
access regime for the Father, including terms and dates, transportation to and
from the visits, pick up and drop off points, including statutory and summer
holidays and vacations.  She provided a comprehensive template for A.D.’s
visits with his Father.

[
20
]

This
comprehensive regime of parenting for the Mother and Father ordered by Ross J.
was never implemented as these Protection proceedings were commenced prior to
the delivery of Justice Ross’ Reasons and resulting Order. With the
commencement of child protection proceedings, the Children’s Law Reform Act
proceedings were stayed by operation of s. 116 (6) of the Child Youth and
Family Services Act.

[
21
]

On
February 1
st
,  2021, the Court placed the child A.D. in the temporary
temporary care and custody of his Mother subject to Society supervision on
terms and conditions pending argument on the Society’s motion with supervised
access to the Father.  On April 8
th
, 2021, Phillips J. made a
temporary Order pending trial having A.D. remain in his Mother’s care and
custody subject to Society supervision on terms and conditions and that
supervised access continue with the Father subject to terms and conditions.  On
November 8, 2021, in the course of this trial, the Society sought to vary the
terms of the prior interim Order relating to the Father’s access. That motion
was dismissed with oral Reasons by Phillips J.

Identification of Issues:

[
22
]

I
have reviewed the written Submissions filed by counsel and I have categorized
the issues before me on the “finding” portion of the hearing as follows:

a.

Is there sufficient evidence on
the balance of probabilities that there is a risk that the child is likely to
suffer serious emotional harm in or more of the following ways:

(i)

Serious anxiety;

(ii)

Depression;

(iii)

Withdrawal;

(iv)

Self-destructive behaviour;

(v)

Aggressive behaviour;

(vi)

Delayed development

b.

Is it fatal to the Society’s case
that the Society has produced no independent, third-party expert evidence that
the child is at risk of suffering the serious harm as described in s. 74 (2)
(h) of the
CYFSA
?

c.

Did the Society engage in a
strategy of selectively disclosing evidence and/or tailoring evidence which can
or could lead to a finding of bias only discoverable under cross-examination
which irreparably tainted the trial process and contributed to the Father’s
difficult and combative conduct during the trial and pushing his level of
frustration beyond reasonable limits;

d.

Are the child’s utterances whether
as to his state of mind or the truth of its contents, it having been agreed by
counsel that these statements met the threshold test of necessity and
reliability, ultimately admissible as necessary and reliable and capable of
sufficient weight to give rise to the finding in “a.” above ?

The Society’s case:

Ms.  S.L.:

[
23
]

The Society’s case consisted of the
observations by the OCL Clinician, Ms. S.L, and the social workers assigned to
work with the Mother and Father, Ms. L.B., Ms. D.C. and Ms. K.C.

[
24
]

The
evidence of Ms. S.L. consisted of a redacted copy of an Incomplete Report as
the Father decided he was no longer interested in completing the OCL process
and no final recommendations were completed.  She was able to make observations
of A.D., what each household offered to him in the way of activities and
housing, contrasted parenting styles and she spoke to A.D. during four
individual visits.  Her observations were subject to cross-examination that I
will detail below.

[
25
]

There
were a number of themes that emerged when she spoke with A.D. He expressed that
he was scared at times of his Father, his Father yelled at him and others at
times, he was afraid of going out on his Father’s boat and although he enjoyed
playing baseball with his Father, he didn’t like running after the balls as
punishment if he failed to hit them. A.D.’s father was clearly very proud of
his abilities at baseball and praised him for his talent.  A.D. was observed as
hesitant and withdrawn with his Father, but he told the clinician that there
were times that he enjoyed his visits with his Father, such as when he went
swimming in the pool with his cousin B. She noted that A.D. did not volunteer
answers when he was around his Father. He had to be prompted by his Father to
do so.

[
26
]

When
A.D. was observed with his Mother, they painted, he was given a choice of what
to play and what colours to choose. In contrast to the Father, the Mother did
not ask A.D. to tell the clinician what he felt or what he liked about
anything.  She, too, praised him for his artwork and choice of colours.  A.D.
was spontaneous and sat in close proximity to his mother.  She observed he
appeared engaged in the choice of activities his mother gave him and he
willingly produced what he was working on with the clinician.

[
27
]

The
evidence revealed that over the course of the clinician’s four (4) individual
visits with A.D. began to open up more about his feelings and concerns. He was
worried that if his Dad found out anything that he said, he (the Dad) would get
mad.  He could not tell his Father he was afraid of riding in the boat, but he
would still go because his Father wanted him to. He could not tell him he
didn’t like chasing the baseballs, as he would get yelled at. He volunteered
that he liked steak, but not the way his father prepared it.  It was too spicy.
He was aware that his Father would return him from his access visit late as
they were watching his cousin’s baseball game.  He also said that when he was
returned from his visits with his Father, his parents did not speak to each
other, and he sighed, but said this was fine.  During his first visit with the
clinician and while at his Mother’s house, he said he wanted to live there. He
described his Mom as good, and his Father was the “bad one”. During his second
visit with the clinician and while he was at his Father’s house, he was worried
that his window was open, and that his Father was listening.  He did express
that he wanted to spend more time with his Mother as she was often working on
the computer as she was at school.  He also expressed that he wanted his Dad to
be nice.  By his third visit with Ms. S.L. , A.D. explained that his Dad had
yelled at him because he (A.D.) told the clinician the truth and he was scared
about the boat as it had flipped over, and they had to hang onto the side of
the boat.  He also said that his father had called him a “pig” and that he used
that word describing his mother, his maternal grandmother, uncle and cousins.
This is when he said he was sad.

[
28
]

During
A.D.’s fourth visit with the clinician while at his Father’s house, this is
when he became upset, started crying, and attempted to cover the phone he was
speaking from with the sleeve of his shirt. His paternal grandmother had
interrupted the visit and wanted the clinician to speak to A.D. while all the
other members of the family were present as “[A.D.] has been told what to
say”.  A.D. was unclear whether his grandmother left the room or if he had
privacy.  This is when the Father entered the room, was not prepared to
continue with the OCL process, told the clinician that A.D. was being
manipulated and  started to yell at the clinician.  The Father denied that he
was yelling and told the clinician that he was taping his conversation with the
clinician.

[
29
]

In
conclusion, at no time did A.D. volunteer that he wanted to live with his
Father.  Her evidence revealed that she was concerned that A.D.’s visits with
her were not private but despite that, she was confident that he had told her the
truth from his perspective.

[
30
]

Cross-examination
of Ms. S.L.  by Father’s counsel revealed that she did not talk about truth and
lies with A.D. and did not ask him specifically about yelling and what that
meant to him. She acknowledged she did not probe A.D. when he said he was
thrown against the wall when he was young.  She explained that her function was
not to investigate; rather she was exploring what A.D. recalled.  She agreed
with Father’s counsel that not everything referred to in her notes or within
quotations in her notes was reflected in her Report.  Cross-examination by
Mother’s counsel and OCL revealed that A.D. was concerned that if she told his
Father what he was saying, his Father would get mad.  She repeated that this
was a common theme by A.D.; fear of reporting, being scared and his
apprehension about lack of privacy at his Father’s home while being interviewed.

[
31
]

In
totality, her Report and her observations were uncompromised in any meaningful
way. Cross-examination by Father’s counsel did not establish or suggest why Ms.
S.L. ’s concerns over A.D’s privacy were unfounded. No specific suggestion was
put to her why or how there was an alternative theory by the Father that his
son was being manipulated, other than the bald claim that the Mother was
telling him to lie and that she was a liar.  She was not compromised on the
critical observation that when the Father terminated the investigation, he was
observed as yelling at her and that he suggested he was taping his conversation
with her.

Ms. K.C.:

[
32
]

The
Society workers each had a distinct role and relationship with the parents and
A.D. Society worker Ms. K.C.  had been assigned to the case as a family
services worker after July 24, 2020.  I would note this was prior to and during
the ongoing custody proceedings and many months thereafter.  She testified in
the course of that trial.  According to Justice Ross’ Reasons, she spoke to her
observations only and “neither party sought to introduce statements made by
[A.D.].” She had interviewed A.D. about five (5) times at the time of her
testimony according to Justice Ross.  Justice Ross’ Reasons reflect that Ms. K.C.
said that A.D. presented as more comfortable at his Mother’s house, that he was
quieter and reluctant to talk at his Father’s house.  Justice Ross noted that
Ms. K.C.’s investigation was not complete, but she had this to say about her
evidence overall: “
Although KC (Ms. K.C.) was a fine witness, there really
wasn’t anything in her evidence from which I could make any conclusions as to
A’s [A.D.]’s best interests.”

[
33
]

The
evidence revealed that Ms. K.C. was working with the Mother and Father and
spoke with A.D. as she was monitoring the unsupervised visits and what was
occurring at the point of access exchange between the Mother and Father.   At
this trial, there were four sources of information relating to her observations
and contacts.  They include her Affidavits of January 25th and June 24
th
,
2021, her case note recordings of April 11
th
, July 23, August 10
th
,
August 22
nd
, October 8
th
, and November 4
th
of
2020 and Recordings of January 4
th
, March 10
th
, April 27
th
,
and May 25
th
of 2021.  Much of this evidence was the subject of
cross-examination by the Father’s counsel.  He asked that these documents be
admitted on the trial.

[
34
]

Initially
A.D.’s visits with his Father were unsupervised as a result of Justice
Phillips’ March 27
th
, 2020 Order.   Much of what A.D. disclosed to
Ms. K.C. had the same themes as what A.D. told Ms. S.L. .  A.D. spoke of being
yelled at and scared of his Father; his Father called him stupid and “not to
act stupid”.  A.D. repeatedly said that he was being asked to tell the lady (the
OCL clinician) that he wanted to stay over or stay with his Father (i.e., to
live with him).  According to A.D., he was asked by his Father and others to
say that on a video and that his Father tried to make a video of him saying
that.  A.D. reported that when he wouldn’t do this on one occasion his Father
threatened to leave him at a beer store and locked him out of his car. This was
apparently sometime around October 2020.  A.D. was also questioned about the
incident in January of 2021.  A.D. said he was pounding on the car door to get
back into his Dad’s car and this scared him.  He said he was crying a lot.  His
Father also yelled at him and said the “s” and “f” word when he wouldn’t do
what his Father wanted.

[
35
]

The
Society’s involvement commenced with a referral from A.D.’s aboriginal
counsellor.  There was an allegation by A.D. that in July of 2020, his Father
had squeezed his neck. Safety plans were developed.  On one occasion when Ms. K.C.
discussed A.D.’s disclosures, the Father confronted A.D., he told A.D. that his
Mother had told him to say these things and A.D. shouted at his Father to stop
raising his voice at him.  A.D. was described as visibly upset by Ms. K.C. as
she was present when this happened.  Generally, and most times when the Father heard
what A.D. was saying, he denied that he was doing anything wrong, he offered
that all of what A.D. was saying was as a result of the Mother’s wrongdoing and
that as far as he was concerned she was putting ideas into A.D.’s mind.  He
also expressed that all of this would be brought to an end when he obtained
custody of A.D. after Justice Ross’ ruling was released.

[
36
]

According
to Ms. K.C.’s testimony and her Affidavits and recordings, all of the above
should not suggest that A.D. did not want to visit his Father; she noted
positive activities such as swimming and Hallowe’en, basketball and baseball.
Her assessment was that the constant questioning of A.D. about sleeping over
and the Father’s conflict with the Mother in the presence of A.D. was impacting
A.D.’s desire to keep seeing his Father.  The Society was waiting to bring a
Protection Application as they wanted to “
await the outcome of the
[custody/access] proceeding and “should [that] outcome … mitigate the safety
risks to [A.D.] then they would not need to bring an Application
”
.

From what I can glean from all this evidence, the Affidavits and the case
recordings, the situation between the Father and the Mother during exchange
times started to deteriorate. Police were called to intervene. Comments such as
“you’re a pathetic Mother” were used by the Father while A.D. was present. The
Mother’s sister was insulted. The Father refused to allow A.D. leave his car to
rejoin his Mother following one such visit. The Father did not want to talk
about the “beer store” incident and he expressed that A.D. was being “mentally
abused”.

[
37
]

Around
the time of these incidents, the Society commenced their Protection Application.
Thereafter, the Father’s visits with A.D. were supervised. The relationship
between the Father and Ms. K.C. continued to worsen. He was angry and upset. He
expressed his belief that his son was being coached and threatened; he
described the Mother as a compulsive liar and he thought by April 2021 he would
have an Order for 50-50 custody of A.D. (I note that this was the second return
date of the temporary care motion before Justice Phillips). He sent vulgar and
insulting text messages to Ms. K.C.; over time their vulgarity and angry tone
increased.   Once A.D.’s visits were supervised at his Father’s home, he
described his visits as “good”, he was having “fun” and a “good time” (these
are his words) and he explained that “there was someone there to make sure his
Father wasn’t yelling at him”.   At the same time, he said that his Father was
“was whispering in his ear that he should say that he wanted to stay over”.  On
the whole after the visits were ordered to be supervised, A.D. was observed as
less stressed and happier.  He was expressing this to Ms. K.C.. His Mother was
observed as less stressed and happier.  She, too, was receiving text messages
from the Father, but she was ignoring them and she was happy she did not have
to worry about conflict occurring in front of A.D. with the access exchanges as
they were now arranged by the Society.

[
38
]

Ms.
K.C.’s cross-examination was conducted by Mother and Father’s counsel and the
OCL counsel, Ms. Kondruk.  Several key areas were clarified in the cross-
examination conducted by the Mother’s counsel and OCL.  Ms. K.C. clarified that
she was physically present when she made the observations she did about A.D.
and his Father about the events of August 23
rd
, 2020.  On this day, there
was a meeting with the Father about A.D.’s disclosures that his Father would
yell at him and tell him to stop lying. She was physically present when he
raised his voice, turned to A.D. and said, “He’s scared to look you in the eye
because he has to go to that shithole, he’s threatened”. A.D. was observed as
quiet, withdrawn and eventually shouted at his Father to stop raising his voice
at him.  She clarified that the Father would refuse to be re-directed when he
would become agitated with her; even raising his voice at her. Other times during
phone conversations, he would hang up on her.  Eventually, Ms. D.C. was
appointed as the Father’s worker as the Father alleged that he was being
“harassed” by Ms. K.C..  In April of 2021 the Father delivered an exceptionally
insulting and potentially threatening email.  The message contained the
following:

“With all due respect, you
can talk to my lawyer if you have anything to say to me. I have nothing to say
to you. You’re lazy, incompetent, failed to do your job and its [sic] pretty

rule in
Browne v. Dunn
.  Asking Ms. K.C. what the investigator meant when

am not entirely sure that it was a reasonable inference to draw from the notes
that what A.D. was saying is that he called the investigator or that the

issue.  At the same time, the court notes that A.D. never wavered from the

[

Father’s insistence that Ms. K.C. should have come to his house and seen his

th

crafted with a focus on the evidence supporting the finding of protection. She
indicated that her practice was to prepare a summary. The case note recordings

Society counsel. Why Society counsel made the choices he did, she did not know.

Affidavit and the one used in support of the temporary care Order. Her trial
Affidavit was used for one purpose; her temporary care motion for another. She

care motion Affidavit that would reduce it length and detail.

[
48
]

for why the case note recordings and her summary of meetings and events would
bear different dates; she explained that the recording program at the Society would

[
49
]

for the suggestion that her Affidavit and her evidence were designed to paint
the Father essentially in a negative light, she rejected this suggestion, referring

fearful.

[
50
]

At
the end of Ms. K.C.’s testimony and after a thorough review of her Affidavits
and the various case note recordings, I was not satisfied that the Father’s
counsel had proved that Ms. K.C. was attempting to tailor her evidence or
selectively disclose the facts that could only be discovered through cross-examination.
To be sure, some of the ambivalence around A.D.’s October 8
th
disclosure
should have been more thoroughly canvassed in her trial Affidavit.  They were more
thoroughly canvassed in her case note recordings.  But as I said above, it is
quite unclear what A.D. was saying about the “beer store” incident and
precisely when it happened.  And Ms. K.C. did not draft the Affidavit placed
before the Court; Society counsel did.

[
51
]

Frankly,
and with all due respect, the problem rests with the preparation of the
Affidavit itself. The Affidavit should have been prepared with considerably
more care and attention to detail.  Leaving it to Father’s counsel to parse out
the numerous recordings to present a more balanced and nuanced account of the
October 8
th
disclosure is an unacceptable practice on the part of
Society counsel.  The Affidavit in question was drafted in the usual Society
style with numerous paragraphs detailing a chronological narrative of case
events.  This makes for unnecessarily lengthy Affidavits lacking in focus and
identification of issues.  However, on the whole I was satisfied, particularly in
reviewing the various case note recordings before the Court and the evidence of
Ms. K.C. herself that she was not biased or trying to withhold critical facts
from the Court.  I was particularly impressed that she was candid in saying
that in hindsight, she could or should have followed up more thoroughly with
A.D. relating to his October 8
th
disclosure, particularly after the
OCL didn’t know if there had been enough time for he and his Father to drive to
a store.  It should be kept in mind that A.D. made a further disclosure about
the beer store incident in early January 2021.  A thorough examination of her
case note recordings reflects that she was careful to document what she asked
A.D.; that she captured A.D.’s responses; that she routinely attempted to
satisfy herself that he understood the difference between a lie or a truth when
she was speaking with him; that she cautioned him on at least one occasion that
it wasn’t necessary to simply tell her “stories” about his Dad.

[
52
]

In
the end,  A.D.’s disclosures of October 8
th
remain a confusing mix
of facts and circumstances that I am not confident can be easily resolved when
they interface with the justice system. The evidence reflects that there have
been multiple interviews with A.D. and Society personnel and multiple
disclosures over time.  A.D. appears to have repeated the allegation again in
January of 2021 as this was all part of his expressed fearfulness and feeling
scared. I do not fault this witness with the manner in which her Affidavit was
prepared.   There was no attempt by this witness to distort the fact-finding
function of this Court.  I find that she was an honest and reliable witness;
she was upset that her Affidavit did not disclose facts that were presented in
her summary to counsel.

[
53
]

I
will address the issue of balanced and sufficiently detailed Society Affidavits
at a later point in this ruling.

Legal Analysis:

On the issue “Did the Society engage in a strategy of
selectively disclosing evidence and/or tailoring evidence which can or could
lead to a finding of bias only discoverable under cross-examination which
irreparably tainted the trial process and contributed to the Father’s difficult
and combative conduct during the trial and pushing his level of frustration
beyond reasonable limits”?

[
153
]

There are three
principles of law that apply to this issue.

[
154
]

First, in
defining the question of bias, the Oxford Dictionary defines “bias” as
“prejudice in favour of or against one thing, person or group, compared with
another, usually in a way considered to be unfair. Other dictionary descriptors
of bias include words like: prejudice, partiality, partisanship, favouritism
and unfairness.   Bias is part of the overall function that a trier of fact
must address in assessing the concepts of witness credibility and reliability.
Such assessments include a broad range of factors which address the
trustworthiness of an individual.   Credibility or honesty speaks to a witness’s
sincerity, candour and truthfulness in the witness box.
Reliability refers to a complex mixture of cognitive, psychological,
developmental, cultural, temporal and environmental factors that impact on the
accuracy of a witness’s perception, memory and ultimately, their testimony.

[
155
]

Secondly, in addressing the issue of why the witness K.C.’s Affidavit
in support of the temporary care motion was different than her trial Affidavit
it is important to recall what Katarynych J. had to say in
Children’s Aid
Society of Toronto v. M.(A.)
,
2002 CanLII 45665
(Ont. C.J.) in addressing
the reduced evidentiary test of credible and trustworthy evidence within the
context of a temporary care motion.  She said that “…
evidence available may
change over the lifespan of a child protection case… At the early stage of a
case the evidence may be based merely on a belief about risk. However, whether
there are reasonable grounds to believe a child is in need of protection is an
“ever-evolving question”. The investigation is “seldom completed at the time of
the motion hearing. The Society’s case reflects what the investigation has
yielded to that point in time”.
(para [16]).

[
156
]

Lastly in
Durham
Children’s Aid Society v. G.S. and T.A.
,
2022 ONSC 547 (CanLII)
, 2022 ONSC 0547 Finlayson J.
identifies some fundamental principles that apply to Society proceedings and
are equally applicable in this matter.  In
Durham
, the Applicant Society
took a number of unusual steps which included withholding evidence in
connection with a Protection Application relating to the Father while a police
investigation was ongoing.  They also withheld serving the parents with
additional Affidavit material once it was available.  The Court found that it
is a matter of fundamental fairness and consistent with Charter principles and
values that notice and evidence be provided to parents at the outset of
proceedings. Justice Finlayson found balanced Affidavits as key to the
Society’s obligations. Referring to the decision of Sherr J. in
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. B.H. and M.P,

[2007] O.J. No. 2446 (Ont. C.J.)
“
The
Society’s role in presenting a case to the court is not merely to present
evidence that justifies their position, but to present all relevant and
probative evidence, including that not favourable to their position, to ensure
that the best possible decision for children can be made … It is not good
enough to say that it is the job of the parents’ lawyers to produce this
evidence. Parents’ counsel (if the parties even have counsel) rarely have the
resources of the Society and should not have to chase after this information.
Child protection trials are not and should not be a game”.
(para [55]).
Succinctly put, the Society has an obligation to put balanced information
before the Court at all times.

On the issue of “Are the child’s
utterances whether as to his state of mind or the truth of its contents, it
having been agreed by counsel that these statements met the threshold test of
necessity and reliability, ultimately admissible as necessary and reliable and
capable of sufficient weight to give rise to the finding of protection?

[
157
]

The issue of the
out of court testimony by a child witness is a complex one.  With the passage
of time and new developments related to the admission of hearsay evidence on a
“principled” basis, the critical issue at all times is whether the evidence can
be said to be necessary and reliable (this is described as a threshold inquiry)
and capable of sufficient weight and reliance (substantively or ultimately
reliable).   In this area of law, other collateral issues involve how and why
the statements are being adduced. Are they simply part of a narrative presented
by a third-party witness which does not offend the hearsay rule as the
statement is tendered for the purposes of context only?  Are they adduced to
support a “state of mind” of the child which evidence again does not offend the
hearsay rule as it is a categorical exception to the hearsay rule.  Lastly, if
the statement
is
adduced for the truth of its contents then the
presumptive rule against admission of hearsay applies and the two-part analysis
applies. In this case, counsel agreed that threshold reliability which
addresses the question of necessity and reliability was agreed upon. Given that
consent, the issue of ultimate or substantive reliability of A.D.’s utterances
rests with me, the trier of fact in determining whether the evidence should be
relied on and its probative value.

[
158
]

A very useful
analysis of the law governing this area is found by Zisman J. in
Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. N.N. and D.G.
,
2019 ONCJ 8
.  I adopt
her reasoning and rationale in its entirety. (paras [63 – 113])

On the issue of “Is there sufficient
evidence on the balance of probabilities that there is a risk that the child is
likely to suffer serious emotional harm in or more of the following ways: (i)
Serious anxiety; (ii) Depression; (iii) Withdrawal;  (iv) Self-destructive
behaviour; (v) Aggressive behaviour; (vi) Delayed development  and  “Is it
fatal to the Society’s case that the Society has produced no independent,
third-party expert evidence that the child is at risk of suffering the serious
harm as described in s. 74 (2) (h) of the
CYFSA
?”

[
159
]

These two issues
are inter-related.

[
160
]

A finding of
protection under s. 74 (2)(h) puts the onus on the Society to prove on the
balance of probabilities that a child is at risk of harm.

[
161
]

There are three
elements to be established:

1.  There has to be a risk that there will be emotional harm;

2.  A child must be at risk of developing
at least one of the harms listed in the section and the degree of harm must be
serious;

3.  The harm identified must result from the actions,
failure to act or pattern of neglect on the part of a parent or a person having
charge of the child.

[
162
]

Risk must be
real and not speculative as not every type and severity of emotional harm is
sufficient to establish the risk of emotional harm justifying state
intervention.  (
Children’s Aid Society of Niagara Region v. P.T.

2003 CanLII 2397 (ON SC)
, 2003,
35 R.F.L. (5
th
) 290 (SCJ family);
Children’s Aid Society of
Ottawa-Carlton v. T. and T.,

2000 CanLII 21157 (ON SC)
, [2000] O.J. No. 2273 (OCJ);
Simcoe Muskoka
Child, Youth and Family Services v. L.V. and D.H
.,
2016 ONSC 7039
(SCJ).
It is not necessary that the Society prove an intention to cause harm; a
Society must prove causation.  A Society can prove causation by act, omission
or pattern. (
Jewish Family and Children’s Services v. K. (R,)

2008 ONCJ
774
(OCJ) affirmed
2009 ONCA 903
.

[
163
]

Risk of harm
must be more than trifling harm; the section uses the word “serious”
demonstrated by one or more of the listed conditions or behaviours. It is not
sufficient for the Society to simply establish that the child is merely sad or
is experiencing some minor emotional unhappiness. (
Jewish Family and Child
Services of Greater Toronto v. Ki. Sl. and Lg. Sl.
,
2017 ONCJ 447
. )

[
164
]

The exposure to
a pattern of parental conflict has been accepted in various cases as creating a
risk of emotional harm.  In
N.N. and D.G
., Zisman J. made a finding of
protection under s. 74 (2) (h) where parental conflict included communication
between parents limited to text and email, where a parent’s conduct included
the making of disparaging comments about the other including Society personnel
and where parental behaviour caused loyalty binds for the children, all the
while refusing to acknowledge the harm that was being done.  In
Simcoe
Muskoka Child, Youth and Family Services v. C.C. and N.N.,
2019 ONSC 4541

a
long history of parental conflict ranging in severity over the years and
including frequent problems with access exchanges and frustration of court
orders supported a
prima facie
case in support of a finding of
protection under s. 74 (2) (h).  In
Ki. Sl. and Lg. Sl.
,
Spence J. found
that a mother’s lack of insight and inability or unwillingness to acknowledge
her daughter’s feelings of stress, fear and anxiety, revealed there was an
ongoing risk of emotional harm to the child. In the circumstances of
Ki. Sl.
and Lg. Sl
., the child repeatedly locked herself in the bathroom to escape
her parent, she withdrew from access, she disclosed constant rages by a parent,
and she stated that she felt unsafe around that parent supported a finding of
serious emotional impact on a child. (para [40]).  In
C.C
. and
N.N.

the child became aggressive and her behaviour and threatened self-harm as a
reaction to her father’s relentless attempts to make her say what he wanted to
hear.  He remained obsessed with the view that the child’s mother had alienated
the child, with no insight into the physical danger or emotional harm he had
exposed her to by his repeatedly trying to get her to acknowledge his belief.
The Father had revoked his consent to enable to child to obtain counselling.
[para 34].

[
165
]

Case authorities
differ on the issue of whether expert evidence on the issue of risk of harm is
required.  In
N.V.C. v. Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto,

2017 ONSC 796 (CanLII)
, [2017] O.J. No. 525 (SCJ) Wilson J. seems to suggest that a court is precluded
from deciding that a child is at risk of emotional harm without evidence from
an expert
.  However, Quinlan J. in
Children’s Aid
Society of Ottawa v. P.Y.,

2007 CanLII 14325 (ON SC)
,
2007 CanLII14325
(SCJ)
opined that expert
evidence will
sometimes
be required to establish a risk of emotional
harm, but it is not a necessary prerequisite. [para 18]. Also
see
Children’s
Aid Society of Ottawa v. P.Y
.
, 2007 CanLII 14325 (SCJ) [para 31 and 32].

[
166
]

On the other hand,
expert evidence is not always required.  Spence J. differed from Wilson J. in
N.V.C.

In
Chukwunomso v. Ransome
,
2017 ONCJ 121
Spence said: “
Courts will
often make decisions about emotional harm – or risk of emotional harm to a
child based on a panoply of evidence. That panoply
may
include an
expert’s report.”
In
Chukwunomso
he continued with the opinion that
the presence or absence of an expert’s report was neither conclusive nor
mandatory to allow a court to arrive at a correct conclusion. He opined that
judges should employ intelligence and common sense in drawing logical
inferences from their general understanding of life itself. [see footnote 5]
In
N.N
., Justice Zisman relied on evidence from several experienced
family service workers who expressed serious concern about the risk of emotion
harm. She also drew on her own common-sense conclusion that children exposed to
years of domestic violence, turmoil and conflict in the parent’s relationship
and have been the subject of litigation for the last 4.5 years and subjected to
numerous investigations were at risk of suffering emotional harm. [para 206].
Further, evidence of a child’s distressed reactions to parental behaviour was
sufficiently clear that a finding can be made without the opinion of an expert:
see
P.Y
);
S.(D.), Re
(2001),
2001 CanLII 28177 (ON SC)
, 14 R.F.L. (5th) 414 (Ont. S.C.);
Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. L.(C.),

2002 CanLII 49693
(Ont.
S.C.); and
Ki. Sl and Lg. Sl.
In
A.B.C. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney
General),

2011 NSSC 475 (CanLII)
the Court found that experts are not
required to establish…psychological and emotional harm…The Court is entitled to
take judicial notice that such effects can be expected albeit they may not
occur in every case [para 50].

[
167
]

In
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.P
.,
2020 ONCA 208
, the Ontario Court of
Appeal rejected an argument that the court must have expert evidence and found
that the risk of emotional harm was well supported in the evidence and was
entitled to deference. [para 6]. The argument had been made that in the absence
of expert evidence that the CAS had not met its burden to show the children
would likely suffer a risk of emotional harm and that except in the rarest of
cases, expert evidence was required.

:

note, I have made considerable effort detailing the evidence, the examinations

nd

The question of ultimate admissibility of A.D.’s
utterances:

[
176
]

I find the
Society met the burden of proving A.D.’s out of court statements and met the
ultimate test of admission on the basis of their ultimate necessity and
reliability.  As I previously said, the issue of threshold reliability and
necessity was conceded. The question was what weight, if any, I would give to
what A.D. was telling the OCL investigator, the OCL clinician and the Society
social workers.

[
177
]

I find that it
was reasonably necessary for A.D.’s out of court statements to be admitted and
that he should not have to testify.  His Father would have cross-examined him
on his statements that he was scared, that he was fearful, that there was
yelling going on at his Father’s house, that his Dad was bad, that his Dad kept
wanting him to say he wanted to stay over or live with him, that his Dad said
he [A.D.] was lying and to stop lying; that his Mother put him up to this and

[
178
]

heard before me and the Father’s own testimony leads me to conclude that the

his sense of reality and he does not accept information from anyone he does not
agree with.  Unless A.D. acknowledged what his Father wanted him to say, the
Father would not accept his explanation.  I find A.D. would have been exposed
to yet more harm and more and more questioning.  He may also be so fearful that

or cry or shout back at his Father if the Father suggested he was lying, as the

more upset and risk of harm

]

th
visit.
She acknowledged she didn’t question A.D. about the difference between and
truth and a lie.  She offered that hers was not a full Ministry interview.
Again, I do not find that this witness was tailoring her evidence to distort
the truth about the Father and A.D.’s relationship.  She was quick to
acknowledge any inaccuracy in her Affidavit or corrections arising from her
notes.  Her account was detailed and fair. This is despite the fact that the
Father told her to “fuck off” when she didn’t see any reference to A.D. ever telling
anyone that he wanted to stay with his Father.

[
188
]

As for the
Updated Society Evidence entered by way of an agreed summary of Facts, I cannot
conclude that this evidence was tailored and/or tainted to cast the Father in a
bad light.  This evidence was entered on consent and without any cross-examination
by Father’s counsel. The summary discloses that after the Father’s visits to
A.D. were resumed on November 13
th
, 2021, they were observed as
going well. Two case aides were in attendance, there was positive encouragement
and coaching by the Father with A.D. while they played games and activities.
The Father expressed his love for A.D. and his son was observed as happy and
smiling. There were hugs and by December 2021 A.D. was calling the visits good,
that he wasn’t nervous to visit his Father; he was observed as happy and
enthusiastic with the extended family. The summary details some concerns with
the Father’s conversations with A.D.; his reluctance to have two case aides
present, how he missed a number of visits in December and January and over the
Christmas holiday season.  I do not conclude that this summary distorts or
tailors the truth in order to disparage the Father’s relationship with A.D
.

[
189
]

As for the
evidence of Ms. K.C., I have previously dealt with the issue of the omissions
in her Affidavit and her case note recordings at paragraphs [41] through [52]
of this Ruling. I do not fault her for its lack of care and attention to detail
around the October 8
th
disclosure by A.D. and whether A.D. was taken
to a store and threatened to be left there by his Father unless he told the OCL
investigator that he wanted to live with his Dad.  I have indicated that I
cannot place the same weight in connection with this disclosure by A.D. as
opposed to others; there is simply too much confusion as to what happened and
all its circumstances.  At the same time, I have indicated that I do not find
A.D. to be untruthful. The evidence on this point alone is simply unclear and
confusing.

[
190
]

I do fault
Society counsel with the preparation of Ms. K.C.’s Affidavit as it was clearly
left for Father’s counsel to parse out the numerous recordings to present a
more balanced and nuanced account of this incident.  No Affidavit in child
protection proceedings should merely focus on the evidence that supports a
finding of protection. That is what Ms. K.C. advised she had been told about
its preparation and focus.   This is an unacceptable practice by Society counsel,
and it should be discouraged, and it should cease. These omissions appeared to
fuel the Father’s theory that the positive aspect of his visits with A.D. were
not fairly presented by the Society, but that is simply not the case when I
consider the totality of the Society’s evidence and the totality of Ms. K.C.’s
testimony.

[
191
]

I concur with
Justice Finlayson’s findings in
G.S. and T.A.
that all relevant and
probative evidence, even that which is not favourable to the Society should be
presented.  I accept Ms. K.C.’s explanation that her notes are available to
Society counsel, that she prepares a summary, but she is not the author of the
Affidavit; Society counsel is.  The evidence revealed she did not make the
determination as to what was relevant and probative; Society counsel does.

[
192
]

Adding to this
quagmire is the Society’s approach to Affidavit construction by a series of
chronological narratives of case events which lends unnecessary detail and
length.  I have indicated that the typical Society Affidavit, in the end, with
this type of construction lacks focus and identification of issues.

[
193
]

When I consider
the totality of Ms. K.C.’s evidence, her very detailed note taking of her
interactions with A.D. and her communications with the Mother and Father, I am
satisfied that there was no intent by Ms. K.C. to distort the truth about
A.D.’s relationship with his Father.  Her case notes and her evidence disclosed
the complete story of her interactions and observations of the Father and A.D.
No Affidavit can provide every minute detail of every interaction she had with
the Mother and Father.  I say this in relation to the August 22
nd
visit,
which was not included in her trial Affidavit, but her notes disclosed that
A.D. had disclosed that his father did not hit or hurt him; that his parents
didn’t say bad things about each other, and the visit went well. Frankly no
Affidavit could contain every event or observation contained in Ms. K.C.’s 137
pages of case note recordings. As Ms. K.C. testified, the Affidavit would
simply be too long.  The objective of streamlining trials by the preparation of
an Affidavit in-chief by Society witnesses would be defeated.

[
194
]

I see no fault
with the fact that Ms. K.C.’s Affidavit in support of the temporary care motion
and her trial Affidavit were not entirely similar in every detail.  I do not
find that this is an inconsistency.  There is a good reason for those
differences. The evidentiary test at the time of the temporary motion is
different and the quality of evidence is different; the stage of the Society
investigation is different. The Society’s investigation was not completed at
the time of the temporary motion. This is entirely consistent with what Justice
Katarynych had to say in
M.A
.

[
195
]

Ms. K.C.
explained to my satisfaction how the dates on her case note recordings were
created and she did not alter or delete the recordings once they were entered.

[
196
]

What Ms. K.C.’s Affidavit
revealed was that she did not attempt to discredit the Father as the evidence
reveals that she did not act on every complaint or “story” recounted by A.D.  I
refer to a historical incident of choking that A.D. revealed to her.  She told
A.D. that he didn’t have to come up with stories about his Dad. She encouraged
him to have a positive time with his Father during their visits.  She developed
safety plans for working with the Father and Mother. She did not immediately
commence this Protection Application; she waited months to do so. The Society
expected that the custody/access proceedings between the Mother and Father
might mitigate any risks to A.D. and avoid a Protection Application being
brought.   She noted positive activities such as swimming, Hallowe’en,
basketball and baseball activities between the Father and A.D. It was only
after the unsupervised visits began to deteriorate, when the Father told the
Mother’s sister to “get her fat face back in the car”, when the relentless text
messages by the Father to the Mother described her as “a pathetic excuse for a
Mom”, when access exchanges necessitated police intervention from time to time
and when A.D. continued to express his fearfulness and upset, that the Society
intervened.  Even after A.D.’s disclosures on October 8
th
, 2020,
that his Father had threatened to leave him at the Beer Store unless he spoke
with the OCL investigator, the evidence reveals that Ms. K.C. continued to
encourage A.D.’s access with his father and she encouraged his Mother to do
so.   After the Father’s visits were supervised in February of 2021, Ms. K.C.
testified that A.D. described these visits as “good”, that he was having fun;
that these were good times.

[
197
]

These factors
suggest to me that Ms. K.C. was not biased or unfair to the Father.  Through
her evidence, her case recording which were entered on this trial and her
evidence, she was a fair and objective witness despite the evidence that she
was the recipient of some particularly nasty emails by the Father. He described
her as lazy and incompetent. He told her that his son was suffering emotional
distress and “God will deal with you for that though”.  He claimed she was
harassing him and wanted another worker.  She continued to report to the Father
despite his conduct towards her.

[
198
]

I find no
foundation that the Society is “biased” against the interests of the Father as
a result of another Justice’s ruling in an unnamed case.  Counsel for the
Father provided the Court with a transcript of a Ruling by Vickerd J. in
connection with a motion before her on November 2
nd
, 2021.  She does
find that in the circumstances of the unnamed case that the Society had
tailored its evidence to lead to the conclusion that it was the Father who was
responsible for the adult conflict concerning the children. She refers to
evidence that she opines has been tailored.

[
199
]

With respect,
that case has no connection to the proceedings before me, the issues before me
or the evidence before me.  I had the opportunity to observe the witnesses, to
assess their objectivity, to describe events with detail and to respond
appropriately to cross-examination. They admitted mistakes and made
corrections.  Poor and inadequate construction of a trial Affidavit does not
support a finding of bias.  It does reflect a misunderstanding by Society
counsel as to his role and obligation before the Court in preparing a balanced
Affidavit. This submission however is without merit.

Finding of Protection and Necessity of Expert
Evidence:

[
200
]

I find there is
overwhelming evidence that there is a risk that A.D. is likely to suffer
emotional harm demonstrated by the harms listed in Section 74 (f) (i) to (v) of
the
CYFSA
resulting from the actions, omissions and patterns on the part
of A.D.’s Father.  The primary concern of the Society at the commencement of
the Protection Application related to A.D.’s exposure to his parents’ conflict.
I find that concern has not only continued but has increased as a result of the
conduct of the Father.

[
201
]

The following is
a summary of what the evidence in this matter reveals.

[
202
]

The Father lacks
insight into his behaviour during access exchanges.  He does not acknowledge
that it is fearful and scary to A.D. when he leaves him in the car while
confronting and yelling at the Mother or police, or is forced to hide his head
or that it is upsetting when he (A.D.) and others are being recorded while the
conflict is taking place.  The Father’s position is that the Mother is solely
responsible for the conflict, that all of this will be alleviated if the Mother
only gives him the unsupervised access that Ross J. granted him. To be a good
co-parent he wants the Mother to do exactly what he wants.  The Father’s
behaviour on access exchanges includes delivering A.D. late or making last
minute changes or threatening to not return him at all.  That also means
sending relentless text messages to the Mother if she does not do what he
wants; all the while making disparaging and insulting remarks such as “you’re a
pathetic Mother” or telling his sister-in-law to get her “fat face back into
the car”.  When he cannot reach the Mother as she refuses to answer the phone
as a result of what I consider his abusive behaviour, he contacts police authorities.
He is incensed when the Mother expects some degree of compliance with time and
delivery of A.D. and exits the car with A.D. inside or outside all the while
expressing profanities and anger.  I find that it is the Father who is
responsible for the conflict and has contributed to the Mother’s fear which in
turn has led to numerous contacts with police authorities during access
exchanges all of which exposes A.D. to the risk of serious emotional harm.

[
203
]

The Father lacks
insight into his behaviour directed at A.D. He is relentless in telling A.D. to
tell others that A. D. wants to live with him or stay over at his house rather
than his Mother’s, or telling A.D. that his Mother is a bad parent.  The Father
did this during the time the OCL investigator was completing her report and he
gave A.D. limited privacy when he was speaking with her.   He does this during
access visits when he is being supervised and whispers that he (A.D.) should
say he wants to stay over.  He does this when he calls A.D. a liar “because he
has to go back to that shithole” (referring to his Mother’s house and home).
He doesn’t realize that A.D. is afraid of riding high speeds on his boat or
falling out of boats or chasing baseballs when he misses them. He has called
A.D. a “pig” and “not to act stupid” and the “s” and “f” word.  The Father
doesn’t even realize that A.D. isn’t having a good time at a visit when the
conversation turns to his relationship with his Mother and the Father’s
obsession that the Mother is coaching or manipulating A.D. to say bad things
about him.

[
204
]

The Father’s
lack of insight into his role as a Father is staggering. He considers himself
an amazing Father.  He can’t understand why he is coaching other children at
baseball but A.D. expresses fearfulness of him.  He believes the Mother is
solely responsible for alienating him, that she is responsible for A.D.’s fear
and that she coaches A.D. on what to say.  The Father believes that A.D. will
grow up hating his Mother and will grow up confused and will kill people.  He
describes the Mother as a “psychopathic” and “psychotic” and that “he hates
her”.  He considers the Protection Application a laughing matter and refuses to
acknowledge that the sole custody/decision making remains with the Mother.  He
tells others that he has an order for 50/50 custody and that he has lawsuits
pending against the Society and others.  These actions and steps by the Father
have exposed A.D. to the risk of emotional harm as the Father continues to
expose A.D. to his unfounded opinion that the Mother is turning A.D. against
him, that the Mother is lying, and that A.D. is turn is lying.

[
205
]

The Father does
not appreciate that making disparaging remarks about the Mother or the Mother’s
family puts A.D. in a loyalty bind. Even during supervised visits after A.D.
stopped visiting with him due to his fearfulness and fright, he was heard to
say that “make sure that you use your own words and own voice to speak for
yourself”.  He exclaimed that A.D. gets good food at his house and he wondered
“the last time he had steak like that”.   He called the Mother and her family
“pigs” to A.D. The Father’s own evidence was that the Mother is a “psychopathic
vindictive ex”, that she has mental health issues and was on a lot of meds.
He opined that what A.D. had to say about fearfulness around him was as a
result of her lies, her coaching and parental alienation and abuse.  When the
Mother became upset when the Father held over A.D. on Hallowe’en eve 2020, the
Father said to A.D. “your Mom’s not going to let you go trick or treating”
thereby telling A.D. that the Mother was responsible for the resulting upset.
When A.D. spoke to the OCL clinician he said, “his Father makes him say bad
things about his Mom that are not true”.  He told Ms. D.C. that “my Dad wants
me to think my Mom does stuff and she doesn’t”.  These steps are causing undue
harm and emotional upset for A.D.

[
206
]

The Father’s
lack of acknowledgement of A.D.’s feelings and needs is astonishing. He has no
appreciation of his raised voice or stern manners directed to A.D. and others.
He wants A.D. to like his “spicy” steak.  The Father was willing to forego any
access with he and A.D. between mid-January and early March 2021 as  he was not
prepared to have it supervised at the CAS offices; thus, he didn’t exercise
access to A.D. at all.  The Father also missed visits in late December and over
the Christmas holiday period of 2021.  He missed a January 8th, 2022, visit
with A.D. when no one was at his home.  On June 12th, 2021, the Father became
enraged on reading Affidavits about what A.D. had told others about his feeling
frightened and scared and the Father hurt A.D. while cutting his hair. During
that visit the Father said that “he was done giving up his life for A.D.”,
“that he was done with it” that “he was tired of A.D.’s lies” and that “if A.D.
chose to leave the visit, he will never see his Father again.”  He told A.D.
that he (the Father) was the best in the world, that he was “ungrateful” for
leaving, that he made his grandmother cry and that “A.D. should be careful
leaving as he was being bribed and doing what people told him to do i.e.,
lying”.  This kind of conduct and dialogue persisted throughout the visit; the
Father could not be dissuaded.  He caused emotional upset and harm for A.D.,
did not console him, made him feel guilty over his decision to leave; did not
approach the car where A.D. was seated and remained standing at the household
door, never approaching A.D.  He was incapable of controlling his anger and
upset for the sake of A.D.’s  feelings and emotional wellbeing.

[
207
]

A.D. has
demonstrated emotional harm from this pattern of conduct by his Father. As
early as the time that the OCL investigator was seeing him, he was telling her
he was afraid to speak with her, afraid to tell her what he felt as his Father
would get mad; he was observed as withdrawn and hesitant.  When he told the OCL
investigator about his parents’ access exchanges, he sighed.  He has showed
upset and tears; at times he has been quiet and withdrawn. He has shouted at
his Father to stop raising his voice when he is scared or afraid.  He shouted
at his Father when his Father confronted him over telling Ms. K.C. that he was
afraid of his Father.    On June 12th, 2021, as a result of the Father’s
behaviour he was observed as frozen; he left the visit early, he wanted to
leave and could not be consoled.  Initially he was observed as screaming, then
crying, then nonresponsive and lastly sobbing loudly.  He called his Father a
bad father and he didn’t want to visit him at all initially; later he joined
him in visits as long as he was safe; when he had two case aides supervising
him and his Father.  He is described as scared when the police are present at
access exchanges and when they are at his house for wellness checks at the
Father’s request.

[
208
]

This is a child
who is demonstrating the risk of serious emotional harm as he is showing
behaviour such as terminating visits with his Father and insisting they be
supervised and all the while showing a pattern of serious anxiety and upset,
withdrawal, depressive and aggressive behaviour. He has been observed as quiet
and withdrawn, tearful, scared, fearful, crying and conversely, shouting at his
Father and Father’s family to “stop their yelling” – whatever that means to him.

[
209
]

The risk of harm
to A.D. is serious as the Father does not acknowledge the harm he is causing
and is not prepared to address or change his behaviour.  Most of his promises
in his Affidavit he does not intend to comply with.  He is not prepared to work
with the OCL, with the Society workers or the Mother in controlling his angry
outbursts.   He does not acknowledge that his behaviour is driving A.D. away
from him.  He believes he can ask his son any number of times “why is he lying”
when he doesn’t like what A.D. is saying.  He has that right as his Father, he
said.  He terminated the OCL investigation before its completion. He frustrated
the course of that investigation by interfering with A.D.’s sense of privacy.
At times he would not speak to Ms. K.C. when she attempted to re-direct him or
address her concerns with him.  He forwarded her ugly and obnoxious emails.  He
used a profanity with Ms. D.C. when she did not recall ever hearing A.D. say he
wanted to stay with his Dad.  He refused to be re-directed by Ms. L.B. on June
12th, 2021, with his unacceptable behaviour. He has shouted and used
profanities with police authorities and has been warned to keep the peace in
the course of access exchanges.   He intends to keep calling the police over
wellness checks for A.D. even though this makes A.D. scared.  As irony would
have it, the Father is willing to lie about his criminal record which includes
assaultive behaviour.  He has been prepared to tell the police that his access
is being denied or A.D. is in the company of a drug user, just to secure his
ends.

[
210
]

If ever there
was a case for a finding of a risk of emotional harm where the nature and
degree of harm is serious and high, this is it.  A.D. has been exposed to a
pattern of parental conflict over a number of years where his Mother is fearful
and submissive; where his Father is angry and stern. So long as the Father
refuses to have a lack of regard for the impact of his decisions and actions on
A.D.  This will expose A.D. to an unacceptable risk of harm. So long as the
Father intensifies his campaign to belittle and ridicule the Mother, A.D. will
be exposed to an unacceptable risk of harm. So long as the Father wants A.D. to
say he wants to live with him, this will expose A.D. to an unacceptable risk of
harm.  So long as the Father refuses to work cooperatively with the clinicians
and Society social workers to address his son’s fears and feelings, A.D. will
be exposed to an unacceptable risk of harm.  So long as the Father’s opinions
do not coincide with the views of the professionals and clinicians working with
his son, A.D. will continue at risk of harm.

[
211
]

This is not a
case on the evidence before me that requires expert evidence on the issue of
the risk of emotional harm.

[
212
]

The panoply of
evidence before me together with my own intelligence and common sense tell me
that A.D. is at risk of emotional harm that is serious and demonstrated by
fear, withdrawal, upset and anxiety and emotional withdrawals and now finally
outbursts, over a long period of time. I am satisfied that A.D.’s distressed
reactions to his Father’s behaviour presents a clear and compelling picture
that a finding of protection can be made without the opinion of an expert.
Frankly, A.D. deserves to be safe.

[
213
]

In summary there
shall be a finding of protection under s. 74 (2) (h) of the
CYFSA.
